The separation of powers principle functionally differentiates several types of state power (usually legislation , adjudication , and execution ) and requires these operations of government to be conceptually and institutionally distinct and clearly articulated, thereby maintaining the integrity of each branch. [ 1 ] To put this model into practice, government is divided into structurally independent branches to perform various functions [ 2 ] (most often a legislature, a judiciary and an administration, sometimes known as the trias politica ). When each function is allocated strictly to one branch, a government is described as having a high degree of separation; whereas, when one person or branch plays a significant part in the exercise of more than one function, this represents a fusion of powers . When one branch holds unlimited state power and delegates its powers to other organs as it sees fit, as is the case in communist states , that is called unified power .
